arc-diagram.title: Arc diagram
arc-diagram.description: Places entities in order on a line and joins each related pair with a semicircular arc whose thickness is the value of the connection; dots are sized by each entity's total. Use: Connections among up to about 20 entities that have a meaningful order (stops on a line, chapters, age groups, teams by size): trips between stations, trade between neighbours, characters sharing scenes. Avoid: Flows with a direction through stages (use sankey-chart); one source splitting into parts (use fan-flow); a full matrix of every pair where exact values matter (use heatmap); more than about 20 entities or 60 connections (use heatmap).

area-chart.title: Area chart
area-chart.description: Shows a quantity over time as a filled area from zero: one series, stacked series, shares of 100%, or a streamgraph. Use: A volume or cumulative quantity over time where the filled magnitude matters; stacked when the total and its composition both matter; percent when only the mix matters; stream for the changing mix of many series over a long period. Avoid: Comparing the trajectories of several series against each other (use line-chart: only the bottom band of a stack has a flat baseline); a few time points (use bar-chart with stack); more than about 6 bands.

Use: Showing a distribution while keeping every individual visible: 30 to about 2,000 named things (countries, players, schools), optionally in a few rows by group, with one or two highlighted. Avoid: More than about 2,000 rows or when only the summary matters (use histogram or box-plot); many groups with few rows each (use strip-plot); two numeric measures (use scatter-chart).

Use: Showing the recent history of a number inside a stat tile, a table cell or a sentence, where the shape of the trend matters and exact values do not. Avoid: Anything the reader must read values from or compare across series (use line-chart); fewer than about 5 points (state the change in words or use big-number with a delta).

annotated-timeline.description: A vertical sequence of dated events along a rail, each with a short explanation and, optionally, a small chart or figure. Avoid: More than two states (use `line-chart` or `slope-chart`); many entities each with a before and after (use `dumbbell-chart` or `arrow-chart`); two unrelated figures (use `stat-row`).

Use: Whenever a chart needs its meaning stated in words next to it: the standard chart-plus-interpretation unit of a report. The chart's title states the main fact with its number. The callout adds a second fact, a cause or a caveat in plain words. Avoid: Repeating the chart title in the callout; long narration (put `prose` before the chart instead); a chart that is already a small tile (the callout would outweigh it).

Use: The same entities under two to five measures or scalings where each view changes the reading: total / per capita / change, absolute / share, linear / log. Give the frame a plain label as its title. Each view's `subtitle` names its measure. Avoid: Hiding the most important view behind a tab (show it first, or show both with `small-multiple-grid`); unrelated charts (give each its own figure); more than five views.

comparison-table.title: Comparison table
comparison-table.description: A table whose rows carry inline sparklines, deltas and in-cell bars beside their exact values, from rows and a column config. Use: Comparing five to twenty entities on a level, a trend and a change at once: countries, products, teams. Readers look up their row. The sparkline and delta show how the value changed. Avoid: Plain lookups with no series (use `data-table`); one measure ranked (use `ranked-list` or `bar-chart`); trends the reader must compare precisely (use `small-multiples`). Each sparkline has its own scale, so it shows the direction of change and cannot be used to compare levels between rows.

data.description: Wide data: one row per entity. Long data: one row per entity and period, with `groupBy`. Omit inside `<InsightData>`.

transform.description: Applied before rows are grouped.

columns.description: Columns in order; the first is the row header. `kind` is `text`, `number`, `sparkline`, `delta` or `bar`. For wide data give a sparkline or computed delta its series with `fields`; for long data they use the group's rows.

groupBy.description: Long data: the entity field. Rows sharing a value become one table row, in data order.

highlight.description: Entities to emphasise, matched on the first column.

sort.description: Order rows by a column's value. Default direction: descending. With `sortable` this is the opening order.

sortable.description: Click or press Enter on a column header to sort by it (numbers largest first, text A to Z); a second press reverses and a third restores the original order. Sparkline columns do not sort; set `sortable: false` on a column to exclude it.

limit.description: Show only the first N rows.

title.description: The main fact with its number, or a plain label. Set as the table's `<caption>`.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to the sparklines and deltas.

mode.description: Colour mode.

filter-chips.title: Filter chips
filter-chips.description: The active crossfilter selections of the surrounding `InsightData`, shown as removable chips with a reset control. Use: Inside any `<InsightData>` whose charts use `select`: put it above the charts so readers can see what is filtered, drop one value, or clear everything. `linked-charts` already includes it. Avoid: Outside `<InsightData>` it renders nothing unless you pass `selections` yourself. It is not a filter builder: selections are made by clicking marks in the charts.

selections.description: Selections to show when there is no surrounding `<InsightData>` (or to override it), keyed by owner. Uncontrolled unless `onSelectionsChange` is given.

labels.description: Display names for field names, e.g. `{ region: "Region" }`.

hint.description: Shown while nothing is selected, e.g. "Click a bar to filter".

count.description: Show "1,204 of 5,000 rows" at the end of the line.

theme.description: Theme override.

mode.description: Colour mode.

hero-figure.title: Hero figure
hero-figure.description: The opening exhibit of a piece: kicker, headline and deck above one large chart, with a source line underneath. Use: At the very top of a data story or a one-page report. The headline states the main fact with its number. The chart shows that fact. Avoid: Giving the chart its own `title` (the headline is the title; use the chart's `subtitle` for the measure). A second hero on the same page: later sections use `section` or `chart-callout`.

title.description: The main fact, as one plain sentence with its number.

kicker.description: Small label above the title: the series or topic.

deck.description: One plain sentence under the title that adds a second fact.

date.description: Publication date. ISO dates are formatted for the locale.

chart.description: The hero chart: a spec or a React element, without its own title.

source.description: Where the data comes from. Entries with a `url` are linked.

level.description: Heading level of the title.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to the headline, chart and source note.

mode.description: Colour mode.

kpi-grid.title: KPI grid
kpi-grid.description: A responsive grid of trend cards drawn from one dataset: each metric shows its latest value, its change and a sparkline. Use: The top of a dashboard or a monthly report: three to eight metrics tracked over the same periods. Pass one table with a column per metric. Avoid: Figures without a series behind them (use `stat-row`); comparing the metrics with each other on one scale (use `line-chart` or `small-multiples`); more than eight cards.

data.description: One dataset in time order: a row per period, a column per metric. Omit inside `<InsightData>`.

transform.description: Applied once, before the cards read the rows.

x.description: Period field shared by every metric.

metrics.description: One card per metric; each takes the props of `trend-card`.

compare.description: Baseline for every card's change; a metric can override it.

change.description: Relative change, or the difference between the two values; a metric can override it. An absolute change of a percentage metric is shown in percentage points ("−2.1 pts").

deltaFormat.description: Format for absolute changes, e.g. `"{value} pp"` or `"signed"`; a metric can override it. Default: points for percentage formats, otherwise the metric's own `format`.

columns.description: Preferred columns. Default: up to four, reduced to fit cards of at least 200px.

title.description: The main fact with its number, or a plain label.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to every card.

mode.description: Colour mode.

linked-charts.title: Linked charts
linked-charts.description: Two to four charts over one shared dataset in a responsive grid: clicking a mark in one filters the others, with the active filters shown as removable chips. Use: Exploration of one table along several dimensions: by region, by category and over time. Pass row-level data once; each chart aggregates it with its own `transform`, sets `select: true` and omits `data`. Avoid: A report that states one fixed fact (use `chart-callout` or `scrolly-chart`); charts over unrelated datasets (they cannot filter each other); more than four charts.

data.description: The shared, row-level dataset.

transform.description: Applied once to the shared data.

charts.description: Two to four chart specs or elements. Give each `select: true` (or a field name) and a stable `id`, and leave out `data`.

columns.description: Preferred columns. Default two; fewer when charts would be narrower than `minChartWidth`.

minChartWidth.description: Narrowest a chart may get before the grid drops a column.

hint.description: Shown in the filter line while nothing is selected.
hint.$comment: default: "Click a mark to filter the other charts"

labels.description: Display names for the fields in the chips.

count.description: Show the filtered row count at the end of the filter line.

selections.description: Controlled selections, keyed by chart id.

title.description: Heading for the group.

subtitle.description: Measure, population and period shared by the charts.

before.description: Content rendered inside the shared store above the grid: figures, text, a custom component that calls `useInsightData()`, or a spec that omits `data` (e.g. `stat-row`, `data-table`). It sees the same filtered rows as the charts.

after.description: Content rendered inside the shared store below the grid, e.g. a detail table of the filtered rows.

gap.description: Space in px between the `before` slot, the grid and the `after` slot.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to every chart.

mode.description: Colour mode.

metric-breakdown.title: Metric breakdown
metric-breakdown.description: A headline number with its composition underneath: one segmented bar and a key giving each part's value and share. Use: A total that the reader will immediately want split: a budget by department, revenue by product line, emissions by sector. Two to six parts that add up to the number above them. Avoid: Parts that do not sum to the headline; more than about six parts (use `bar-chart`); composition compared across groups or over time (use `bar-chart` with `stack: "percent"` or `area-chart`).

data.description: One row per part. Omit inside `<InsightData>`.

transform.description: Applied before the parts are summed.

name.description: Field naming each part.

value.description: Field with each part's value.

total.description: The headline number. Default: the sum of the parts.

context.description: The line under the headline number.

delta.description: Change in the headline number. Numbers render as signed percentages.

upIsGood.description: Whether an increase is good news.

show.description: What the key prints beside each part.

sort.description: Order parts by size; the bar and the key follow.

format.description: Number format for the headline and the parts.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to the number and the bar.

mode.description: Colour mode.

poster.title: Poster
poster.description: The sheet an infographic is composed on. It paints a full-bleed ground from a poster theme, forces one theme and colour mode on everything inside, and lays out a masthead, a grid of panels and a footer. It can save the whole sheet as one PNG. Use: Use it as the outer frame of any infographic: one dominant graphic with a few supporting panels, on a painted ground. Give it a poster theme (`noir`, `magenta`, `dusk`, `paper`, `ocean`, `forest`, `blueprint`, `sunrise`) and put a chart or figure spec in each panel. Put the one fact in `title` and keep panel headings short. It reflows to one column under 600px. Avoid: Long reading text or more than about six panels (use `report-page` or `visual-essay`). A single fact at a fixed social size (use `social-card`). Charts that need axes, gridlines and dense labels to be read, because a poster ground suits large flat marks with their values printed on them.

title.description: The poster's one fact, as a plain sentence with its number. Set large and light in the theme's display face.

kicker.description: Small label above the title: the topic or series.

subtitle.description: One or two lines under the title: the measure, population and period.

panels.description: The blocks, in reading order. Each is `{ content, title?, subtitle?, span?, rowSpan?, source?, note?, align?, valign?, bleed?, id? }`. `content` is a component spec or rendered content. `span` is in units of `columns` (default: full width). `bleed` runs the content to the poster's left and right edges.

columns.description: Columns of the layout grid: a 12-unit grid, or a simple count such as 2 or 3. Under 600px every panel is full width; from 600 to 760px the grid has two columns.

gap.description: Space between panels in px. Default 40 (28 under 600px).

padding.description: Space between the poster's edge and its content in px. Default 56 (36 under 900px, 20 under 600px).

maxWidth.description: Widest the poster is drawn. It is centred in wider containers.

aspect.description: Fixed shape as width / height: `0.75`, `"3:4"`, `"16:9"`. The poster still grows when its content needs more height, and the ratio is dropped under 600px.

theme.description: A poster theme name, any other theme name, or a theme object. It is passed on to everything inside.

mode.description: Colour mode of the poster and everything in it. A poster does not follow the page unless you set `auto`. Only `paper` has a different dark variant.

background.description: CSS background of the sheet, a colour or a gradient. Default: the poster theme's ground. Keep it close to the theme's `surface`, which charts use for the gaps between marks.

rules.description: Lines under the masthead, between rows of panels and above the footer.

sources.description: Where the data comes from, shown in the footer.

note.description: Caveat shown in the footer, e.g. "Illustrative data".

credit.description: Who made the poster, shown at the right of the footer.

level.description: Heading level of the title. Panel headings are one level down.

download.description: Show a "Download PNG" control under the poster. The image is the whole sheet, drawn from the DOM onto a canvas, without the control.

exportWidth.description: Width of the downloaded PNG in pixels.

filename.description: File name without extension. Defaults to a slug of the title.

proportion-statement.title: Proportion statement
proportion-statement.description: A share stated as a countable sentence ("37 in every 100…"): a waffle grid or a row of icons beside the statement in large type, with the number emphasised. Use: One proportion that is easier to read as a count of people or units than as a percentage. Round to a small whole first: 1 in 4 with icons, 37 in every 100 with a waffle. Avoid: Several shares side by side (use `bar-chart`, or `waffle-chart` with categories); a precise percentage where the decimals matter (use `big-number`); totals above 100.

value.description: How many of the whole are counted.

figure.description: The emphasised words. Default: "{value} in every {total}", or "{value} in {total}" up to 20.

text.description: The rest of the sentence, read straight after the figure.

visual.description: Grid of cells or row of glyphs. Default: icons up to a total of 20, waffle above.

side.description: Side the visual sits on; under 520px it goes on top.

detail.description: A second, quieter sentence under the statement.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to the visual.

mode.description: Colour mode.

quote-figure.title: Quote with figure
quote-figure.description: A pull-quote paired with the statistic or small chart that backs it up, side by side and stacking in narrow containers. Use: A quotation shown next to the number it refers to: an interview finding with its survey figure, an executive's statement with the metric. One per section. Avoid: A quote with no evidence (use `pull-quote`); a figure that needs axes to read (use `chart-callout` and put the quote in prose); unattributed quotations.

quote.description: The words quoted, without quotation marks.

role.description: Their role, or where it was said.

cite.description: Source URL, linked from the attribution.

stat.description: The statistic that backs the quote up; takes the props of `big-number`.

figure.description: A small chart or figure instead of, or under, the statistic: a spec or a React element.

side.description: Side the evidence sits on; under 640px it goes underneath.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to the quote and the figure.

mode.description: Colour mode.

ranked-list.title: Ranked list
ranked-list.description: A ranking as a list: position, name, value and a thin in-row bar, with an optional change indicator and highlighted rows. Use: A top-N list where the names matter as much as the values: league tables, best and worst performers, leaderboards with a movement column. It keeps long names readable and works in a narrow column. Avoid: Precise visual comparison of many values or more than about 15 rows (use `bar-chart`); several measures per entity (use `data-table` or `comparison-table`); rank changing over time (use `bump-chart`).

data.description: One row per entity. Omit inside `<InsightData>`.

transform.description: Applied before ranking.

name.description: Field naming each entity.

value.description: Field with the value that ranks them. Bars start at zero.

change.description: Field with a change shown at the end of each row: a number (0.12 is +12%) or a string.

changeFormat.description: Format for numeric changes, e.g. `"signed"` for places moved.

upIsGood.description: Whether a positive change is good news.

detail.description: Field with a short secondary line under each name.

sort.description: Order by value; `none` keeps the data order.

limit.description: Show only the first N rows after sorting.

highlight.description: Entity names to emphasise. The other bars are drawn in grey.

max.description: Value at which a bar is full. Default: the largest value shown.

format.description: Number format for the values.

title.description: The main fact with its number, or a plain label.

theme.description: Theme override.

mode.description: Colour mode.

scrolly-chart.title: Scrolly chart
scrolly-chart.description: A scroll-driven story from JSON: one base chart spec and a list of steps, each with narration and a patch of chart props applied while that step is active. Use: Walking a reader through one chart in stages: show everything, highlight the subject, change the measure, add the annotation. Make ONE change per step (the highlight, the data or the encoding) so the reader can see what changed. Avoid: Steps that change several things at once, or that swap to an unrelated chart (start a new `section` instead). More than about seven steps. A fact that one view can show (use `chart-callout`). In documents that will be printed or embedded in a short frame, set `scrollMode: "steps"`.

chart.description: The base chart spec: `{ type, data, x, y, ... }`. Give it a `title`; steps may replace it.

steps.description: The steps in order. `content` is a short paragraph that says plainly what the chart now shows (`**bold**` works). Every other key is a chart prop merged over `chart` for that step: `highlight`, `transform`, `annotations`, `x`, `y`, `title`… Use `null` to remove a base prop. Change one thing per step.

cumulative.description: Each step's patch builds on the previous steps instead of on the base spec alone.

scrollMode.description: `scroll` pins the chart while steps scroll past; `swipe` makes steps swipeable cards; `steps` shows previous/next buttons; `auto` uses scroll, or swipe on narrow touch screens. (Named `scrollMode` because `mode` is the colour mode.)

side.description: Side of the text column in scroll mode. Narrow containers overlay the text on the chart.

stickyTop.description: Offset from the top of the viewport at which the chart pins; set it to the height of a fixed header.

stepHeight.description: Scroll distance per step, as a CSS length.

title.description: Heading above the whole story.

source.description: Shown after the last step as "Source: ...". Prefer the chart's own `source`, which stays visible.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to the chart and the step cards.

mode.description: Colour mode.

section.title: Section
section.description: A story section: a numbered step marker or a headline, introductory prose, then one or more exhibits in a responsive one- to three-column grid. Use: The building block of a longer piece. Each section states one fact with its number in the title, explains it in a paragraph and shows it in one to three exhibits. Use `step` when the sections are read in order. Avoid: The opening of a piece (use `hero-figure`); a single chart with one callout (use `chart-callout` directly); more than three exhibits in one section (split it).

title.description: The section's main fact, as one plain sentence with its number.

step.description: Step number: turns the heading into a numbered chapter marker ("02 — ...").

kicker.description: Small label above an unnumbered heading.

deck.description: One plain sentence under the heading that adds a second fact.

body.description: The exhibits: one slot or several, each a spec or a React element.

columns.description: Columns for the body at full width; reduced under 720px and 520px.

level.description: Heading level.

id.description: Anchor id for deep links.

spacing.description: Vertical rhythm between heading, intro and body.

children.description: JSX alternative to `body`; each child becomes a grid item.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to everything inside.

mode.description: Colour mode.

small-multiple-grid.title: Small multiple grid
small-multiple-grid.description: Repeats any chart spec once per value of a facet field, each panel with its own filtered rows and a title, in a grid that follows the container width. Use: Faceting a chart form the `small-multiples` atom does not draw: stacked bars, scatter plots, donuts, waffles, dumbbells, histograms. Also when each panel should be a full chart with its own tooltip and axis. Avoid: Line, area or bar facets that must share one value scale: use the `small-multiples` atom, which draws every panel in one chart on a common axis. Here each panel scales to its own rows unless the spec fixes the axis (for example `option: { xAxis: { max: 70 } }`), so say so in the subtitle or fix it. More than about twelve panels.

data.description: Rows for every panel together. Omit inside `<InsightData>`.

transform.description: Applied before the rows are split by `facet`.

facet.description: Field whose values each get a panel.

chart.description: The chart repeated in every panel: a spec without `data` and without a `title`, or a render function from JSX.

columns.description: Preferred columns. Default: up to four, reduced to fit `minPanelWidth`.

minPanelWidth.description: Narrowest a panel may get before the grid drops a column.

order.description: Panel order: data order, alphabetical, or an explicit list of facet values.

panelHeight.description: Plot height of each panel when the spec sets none.

highlight.description: Passed to every panel as its `highlight`, so the same entity is emphasised everywhere.

emphasis.description: Facet values whose panel titles are emphasised.

legend.description: One shared colour key above the panels (`legend-key` items, in series order). Set `legend: false` in the chart spec so panels do not repeat it.

level.description: Heading level of the panel titles.

title.description: The main fact with its number, or a plain label.

subtitle.description: Measure, population, period, and whether the panels share a scale.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to every panel.

mode.description: Colour mode.

stat-row.title: Stat row
stat-row.description: Two to five key figures in one row separated by hairlines, collapsing to two columns and then one as the container narrows. Use: The opening summary of a report or dashboard: the two to five most important numbers. Give every figure a delta or a context line, and order them by importance. Avoid: More than five figures (use `kpi-grid`), a single lead number (use `big-number` with `size: "hero"`), or figures that need their history shown (use `kpi-grid`, or `variant: "tiles"` with a `trend`).

items.description: Two to five figures, most important first. Each takes the props of `big-number` (or `stat-tile` when `variant` is `tiles`).

variant.description: Open figures divided by hairlines, or bordered tiles that can carry a `trend`.

format.description: Number format for every figure that does not set its own.

title.description: The main fact with its number, or a plain label.

subtitle.description: Population and period the figures share.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to every figure.

mode.description: Colour mode, passed on to every figure.

trend-card.title: Trend card
trend-card.description: A KPI card computed from a series: the latest value, its change against a baseline in the same data, and a sparkline of the series. Use: A metric whose recent history matters as much as its level: users, revenue, response time. Pass the series and field names; the figure, the change and the sparkline all come from the same rows, so they cannot disagree. Avoid: A number with no history (use `big-number` or `stat-tile`); several metrics from one dataset (use `kpi-grid`); a series the reader must read values from (use `line-chart`).

label.description: What the figure measures, sentence case.

data.description: Rows in time order, one per period. Omit inside `<InsightData>`.

transform.description: Applied to the rows before anything is computed.

y.description: Value field: the series drawn and the source of the figure and its change.

x.description: Period field, used to name the baseline and in the sparkline tooltip.

value.description: The figure shown. Default: the last row's `y`.

delta.description: The change shown. Default: computed from the series according to `compare`.

compare.description: Baseline for the computed change: first row, previous row, or a number of rows back (12 for year-on-year in monthly data).

change.description: Relative change, or the difference between the two values (use for rates and shares). An absolute change of a percentage is shown in percentage points.

deltaFormat.description: Format for a computed absolute change, e.g. `"{value} pp"` or `"signed"`. Default: points ("+1.9 pts") when `format` is a percentage, otherwise `format`.

deltaLabel.description: What the change is against. Default: "since {first period}" when `x` is given.

upIsGood.description: Whether an increase is good news; decides the delta colour.

context.description: A line under the figure that gives it meaning.

format.description: Number format for the figure and the sparkline tooltip.

kind.description: Sparkline form: a line for a trend, bars for discrete counts.

area.description: Light fill under the line; the scale then includes zero.

trendPosition.description: Where the sparkline sits; `right` falls back to `bottom` in narrow cards.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to the tile and sparkline.

mode.description: Colour mode.

atlas-poster.title: Atlas poster
atlas-poster.description: A landscape spread of up to eleven small illustrations of one subject, each a different graphic form, in three bands of unequal panels: a statement in large type, spokes round an icon and a network of circles; a smooth trend with its peak labelled, nested squares and a slope chart; a pill ranking, a treemap, a tile map and sized circles; and a closing row of icon statements. Use: Use it when one subject has many small facts of different kinds (shares, places, a trend, a change, a ranking, a map) and none of them should dominate: a crop, an industry, a service, a country's internet. Fill at least eight regions. Give every panel a short heading that states its one number. Every region is optional, and each band shares its width among the panels that are present. Avoid: One dominant fact or graphic (use `count-poster`, `flow-poster` or `ranking-poster`). The same measures across several entities (use `matrix-poster`). Fewer than six panels (use `poster` and place them yourself). A phone-first piece: the spread becomes one long column under 600px.

statement.description: Band 1, left: the subject's main number in large light type, in the accent colour.

spokes.description: Band 1, middle: 4 to 12 attributes as spokes round a centre icon (`radial-spokes`).

network.description: Band 1, right: named places or things as circles sized by value and joined by lines (`bubble-network`).

trend.description: Band 2, wide: one measure over an ordered dimension as a smooth filled curve (`area-chart`). The highest point is labelled with its value and position; `peak` replaces that label, and `peak: false` removes it.

area.description: Band 2: two or three quantities as squares nested from one corner, with a bracket stating the ratio (`proportional-area`, `layout: "nested"`).

slope.description: Band 2: each entity at two dates, joined by a line and labelled at the end (`slope-chart`).

rank.description: Band 3: a ranking of 4 to 6 rows as centred pills (`pill-rank`). Pass a `bar-chart` spec for bars instead.

parts.description: Band 3: the parts of one whole as tiles (`treemap`).

map.description: Band 3: a tile map shaded by value (`choropleth-map`). Give every row `col` and `row`, the tile's place in the grid, and the template builds the squares; `code` names the field printed on each tile. Pass `geo` to use your own GeoJSON.

circles.description: Band 3: two to four magnitudes as sized circles (`stat-circles`).

stats.description: Closing row: up to three "3 in 10" statements, each a row of icons with some filled (`icon-stat`).

title.description: The poster's one fact, as a plain sentence with its number.

kicker.description: Small label above the title: the topic.

subtitle.description: One line under the title: the measure, population and period.

theme.description: Poster theme: `noir`, `magenta`, `dusk`, `ocean`, `forest`, `blueprint`, `sunrise`, `paper`, any other theme name, or a theme object.

mode.description: Colour mode of the poster and everything in it. A poster paints its own ground and does not follow the page unless you set `auto`. Only `paper` has a different dark variant.

download.description: Show a "Download PNG" control under the poster that saves the whole poster as one image.

maxWidth.description: Widest the poster is drawn. It is centred in wider containers.

linked.description: Make the marks clickable. Clicking a mark in one graphic highlights the same name in every other graphic that has it, and filters the graphics that read the shared `data`. Click it again, or the empty ground of that graphic, to clear.

data.description: Rows shared by every region whose config leaves out its own `data`. With `linked`, a click filters those regions.

sources.description: Where the data comes from, shown in the footer.

note.description: Caveat shown in the footer, e.g. "Illustrative data".

credit.description: Who made the poster, shown at the right of the footer.

level.description: Heading level of the title. Panel headings are one level down.

comparison-brief.title: Comparison brief
comparison-brief.description: A compared with B on one page. It has a headline that states the result, the headline figures mirrored either side of their labels, one hero exhibit that shows both sides, paired exhibits on a shared scale, a verdict callout and a source note. Use: Use it for two things a reader has to choose between or compare, such as two countries, two products or a before and an after. Write the result with its number in the headline. Put the four or five most important measures in `figures`. Use a two-series line, dumbbell, slope or `before-after` as the hero. In each pair, use the same chart form and the same scale for both sides. The `subject` side takes the accent colour everywhere and the other side stays grey. Avoid: Three or more things (use a `comparison-table` or `small-multiple-grid` inside a `report-page`). One thing over time with nothing to compare it with (use `timeline-story`). Paired charts on different scales, because readers compare bar lengths across the pair.

title.description: The result of the comparison, as one plain sentence with the number in it.

kicker.description: Small label above the title.

a.description: Side A, shown on the left.

b.description: Side B, shown on the right.

subject.description: The side the piece is about. It takes the accent colour; the other stays grey. Match it with `highlight` in the charts.

figures.description: Headline measures. Numeric values get mirrored bars scaled within each row; `better` sets the stronger value bolder.

hero.description: The exhibit that shows both sides at once. Default height 360px.

heroText.description: One or two sentences under the hero.

pairs.description: Paired exhibits under one heading. A is on the left and B on the right; they stack in narrow containers. Use the same form and scale for both.

verdict.description: The closing recommendation, shown as a callout.

sources.description: Where the data comes from, shown in the closing source note. Entries with a `url` are linked.

method.description: How the numbers were produced: definitions, adjustments, exclusions.

note.description: Caveats the reader should know, e.g. "Illustrative data".

credit.description: Who made the piece.

level.description: Heading level of the title; section headings follow one level down.

maxWidth.description: Widest the piece may get. It is centred in wider containers.

theme.description: Theme override, passed on to everything inside.

mode.description: Colour mode, passed on to everything inside.

count-poster.title: Count poster
count-poster.description: A poster that counts at scale. Blocks of thousands of unit icons fill most of the sheet, a second band counts reference groups with the same icon at the same size in a muted colour, and a bottom row holds three small graphics: squares sized by area with a ratio bracket, thick bars with the numbers inside, and shares as nested outlines or filled silhouettes. Use: Use it when the subject is a large count of people or things in 2 to 6 groups and the reader should see the crowd: pupils by stage, trees planted by species, vehicles built by model. Give `hero` the groups and `reference` one to three quantities to compare them with. Both bands use the same `unit`, `icon` and icon size, so their areas compare. State the total in the title. Avoid: Counts under a few hundred (use `pictogram-chart` in a `poster`). Shares of one whole as the main point (use `waffle-chart` or `treemap`). A ranking of many named things (use `ranking-poster`). A flow from sources to destinations (use `flow-poster`).

data-explorer.title: Data explorer
data-explorer.description: A set of linked charts over one shared dataset that filter each other. It has a headline, a sentence of instructions with filter chips, a row of figures that recompute from the filtered rows, two to four charts and an optional detail table. It opens on selections the author chooses. Use: Use it when readers will want to filter the data themselves after seeing the main finding. State the finding with its number in the headline. Set `initialSelections` so the piece opens on the view the headline describes. Use the figures and the `finding` callout to give the numbers for that view. Keep to one dataset and two to four small, plain charts. Readers click the charts to filter, so keep them all the same size. Avoid: A fixed message that needs no exploration (use `executive-brief` or `visual-essay`). Charts over unrelated datasets, which cannot filter each other. More than four charts or five figures.

executive-brief.title: Executive brief
executive-brief.description: A one-page summary. It has a headline that states the main finding with its number, a deck, a row of three or four key figures, one hero chart with a takeaway callout, two smaller supporting exhibits, a short list of actions and a source note. Use: Use it when a decision-maker will spend about a minute on the page. State the main finding with its number and period in the headline. The headline and the hero chart should be enough for a reader who stops there. The figures, supporting exhibits and actions add detail. Use one accent colour for the subject (`highlight`) and leave everything else grey. Mark the cause on the hero as an annotation. The proportions suit a printed page. Avoid: More than one hero or more than three supporting exhibits (use `report-page`). A recurring set of numbers with no single finding (use `scorecard`). A story told in several steps (use `visual-essay`).

explainer.title: Explainer
explainer.description: A vertical infographic in one narrow column. It opens with a big number or a proportion statement (`hook`), then the hero exhibit, then numbered sections with one exhibit each, a conclusion with an optional link, and sources. Use: Use it to explain one subject to a general audience in a single narrow column. The column also works as a tall image or on a phone screen. State the main finding with its number in the headline and repeat the main number in `hook`. Make the hero exhibit the largest thing on the page. Give each numbered section one heading, one exhibit and one sentence with its main number. Write each section so it can be read without the others. Keep one accent colour on the subject (`highlight`) throughout. Avoid: Findings that need caveats and separate interpretation (use `report-page`). A chart that has to change step by step (use `visual-essay` with a scrolly block). More than five sections, because readers stop before the end.

flow-poster.title: Flow poster
flow-poster.description: A portrait poster of where something comes from and where it goes, in three stacked bands painted in one colour: the producers as large labelled tiles, the leading producer's output fanning out as ribbons to an aligned column of destinations, and the destinations as bubbles on a scale of how much each depends on that producer. Use: Use it when one producer leads and the reader should follow its output: ports and the buyers of one port's catch, regions and the users of one region's electricity, terminals and the routes out of the largest. Give `producers` 4 to 10 rows, `flow` 4 to 12 destinations of the leading producer, and `scale` the same destinations with a share (position) and a size. Keep the destination names identical in `flow` and `scale` so `linked` can join them. Avoid: Flows through more than one stage or between many sources and many destinations (use `sankey-chart` in a `poster`). A count of people or things (use `count-poster`). Many measures of the same entities (use `matrix-poster`).

lead.description: The producer the flow starts from. Default: the largest row of `producers`. It names the block the ribbons leave.

flow.description: Middle band: one ribbon per destination, as thick as its value, ending at a column of names, values and shares (`fan-flow`).

scale.description: Bottom band: one bubble per destination, placed by `value` on a 0 to 100 scale and sized by `size` (`bubble-scale`). Set `domain` and `ticks` for a scale that is not a percentage.

format.description: How to print the quantities of the top and middle bands, e.g. `"{value} kt"`.

matrix-poster.title: Matrix poster
matrix-poster.description: One wide landscape graphic that compares 4 to 12 entities on five to seven measures: two measures as S-curves between parallel scales on the left, joined to a table on the right in which every other number is drawn as dots, squares, icons, a ring, a circle or a bar. Both halves share one row order and one colour per entity. Use: Use it for profiles of a handful of comparable things with measures in different units: cities, species, products, stations, teams. Pass one row per entity with every measure in it. Put the two measures whose relationship matters in `curve` and the rest in `columns`, choosing a counted glyph (`dots`, `blocks`, `icons`) for small whole numbers, `ring` for shares, `bar` or `circle` for magnitudes. Leave `highlight` out to give every entity its own colour, derived from the theme when its palette is smaller than the number of entities; set it to draw one or two entities in colour and the rest in grey. Avoid: One measure across entities (use `pill-rank` or `bar-chart`). More than 12 entities (use `data-table` or `heatmap`). A subject with a total and its parts (use `ranking-poster` or `flow-poster`). A phone-first piece: the table stacks into cards under 600px and the poster becomes long.

network-poster.title: Network poster
network-poster.description: A poster of who is connected to whom: a full-width arc diagram with one arc per connection, as thick as its value (`arc-diagram`), a strip of two to four large figures, and a bottom row where the same entities return as circles joined by lines (`bubble-network`) and as a ranking of centred pills (`pill-rank`). Use: Use it when the connections between 5 to about 20 named things are the subject: ferry crossings between harbours, joint papers between institutes, freight between rail yards. Give `hero` one row per connection and the `order` the entities sit in, `map` the entities with a size and optional hand-placed `x` and `y`, and `rank` one measure of each entity. With `linked`, a click on an entity in any of the three highlights it in the other two. Avoid: A flow from sources to destinations in one direction (use `flow-poster` or `sankey-chart`). More than about 20 entities or 40 connections, because the arcs cover each other. Entities with no meaningful order and few links (use `bubble-network` in a `poster`). Parts of one subject (use `radial-poster`).

figures.description: Two to four large figures in a strip under the hero.

map.description: Bottom left: the entities as circles sized by `value` and joined by `links: { from, to, value? }[]` (`bubble-network`). `x` and `y` (0 to 100) place the circles by hand.

rank.description: Bottom right: the entities ranked by one measure as centred pills (`pill-rank`). With only one of `map` and `rank`, that one takes the full width.

profile-poster.title: Profile poster
profile-poster.description: A poster that describes one subject from four sides: the subject as one large silhouette filled to a share (`shape-fill`), two to four large figures, its place among other things on one scale (`scale-ladder`), and a table that sets it beside its peers with every number drawn as a small form (`glyph-table`). Use: Use it for a fact sheet about one named thing: a vehicle, a reservoir, a building, a machine, a species. Give `portrait` one row with the share that defines the subject and the `icon` that stands for it, `figures` the numbers a reader should take away, `scale` the subject among 4 to 10 reference points, and `table` the subject beside 2 to 6 peers. Highlight the subject in `scale` and `table`. On a sheet at least 960px wide the silhouette, the figures and the scale stand in three columns. Avoid: Several subjects of equal weight (use `glyph-table` in a `poster`, or `ranking-poster`). A subject whose parts are the point (use `radial-poster`). A subject with no defining share: leave `portrait` to a full spec such as `stat-circles`, or use `scale-poster` when the scale is the whole subject. Change over time (use `timeline-poster`).

radial-poster.title: Radial poster
radial-poster.description: A poster with one subject in the middle of the sheet: a wheel of spokes round an icon (`radial-spokes`), two to four large figures standing either side of it, and a bottom row with the same subject's surroundings on concentric rings (`orbit-chart`) and a ranking as centred pills (`pill-rank`). Use: Use it when the poster is about the 4 to 12 parts, causes, effects or scores of one thing: what a household's water goes on, the species one tree supports, where one home's energy goes. Give `hero` the spokes and an `icon` for the centre, state the total in the title, and use `figures` for the two to four numbers a reader should take away. Avoid: Parts of a whole that must be compared precisely (use `bar-chart` in a `poster`). Positions on one scale (use `scale-poster`). Change over time (use `timeline-poster`). Connections between many things (use `network-poster`). Large counts shown as crowds (use `count-poster`).

ranking-poster.title: Ranking poster
ranking-poster.description: A poster of one subject by the numbers, in four rows: two figures in large type or as filled silhouettes, two treemaps side by side, a full-width ranking of centred pills with one row highlighted, and packed circles with icons beside a column of sized circles and a closing figure. Use: Use it for a profile of one event, place or organisation that has a headline total, two ways to split it, a ranking of 6 to 12 named things and a few supporting magnitudes: a festival, a race, a nature reserve, a library service. Put the total in the title and repeat it as the first figure. Highlight the ranking row the heading is about. Avoid: A subject whose point is a count of people or things (use `count-poster`). Several entities compared on the same measures (use `matrix-poster`). Eight or more small graphics on one subject (use `atlas-poster`). A ranking alone (use `pill-rank` in a `poster`).

report-page.title: Report page
report-page.description: A section of an analytical report laid out as a document. It has a title block, a summary, numbered findings, then method, limitations and sources. Each finding has one exhibit, an observation and a separately labelled interpretation with a confidence rating and a caveat. Use: Use it for readers who will check the reasoning, as in evaluations, research notes, audits and experiment write-ups. State the main finding with its number in the title. Put all the main findings and the recommendation in the summary. Write each finding title as one fact with its number, and give it an exhibit that shows that fact. Put what the data shows in `observation` and what you infer from it in `interpretation`. End with method, limitations and sources. Avoid: A decision-maker who wants only the result (use `executive-brief`). A general audience (use `explainer` or `visual-essay`). Findings without an exhibit. Put those in the summary.

scale-poster.title: Scale poster
scale-poster.description: A tall poster that is one illustrated scale: a full-height `scale-ladder` with icons, leader-labelled items and named zones, and a narrow side column of large figures and one small graphic, each set level with the part of the scale it describes. Use: Use it when the positions of 6 to about 16 named things on one scale are the whole subject: depths, altitudes, temperatures, distances, ages. Give the scale's rows and zones in `scale`, up to five `figures` with the scale position each belongs to, and optionally a `side` graphic of two to four magnitudes. Beside the scale the figures line up with their positions; under 760px they move below it. Avoid: Comparing sizes rather than positions (use `ranking-poster` or `count-poster`); change over time (use `timeline-poster`); more than about 16 items, because the labels run together; several unrelated graphics (use `poster` and lay the panels out yourself).

scale.description: The scale. A compact `scale-ladder` config: `{ data, name, value, iconField?, icon?, direction?, scale?, min?, max?, ticks?, zones?, scaleLabel?, format?, highlight? }`. Or a full spec, which replaces the ladder.

figures.description: Large figures for the side column. `at` is the position on the scale the figure belongs to; beside the scale the figure is set level with it under a dotted rule.

side.description: One small graphic in the side column. A compact `stat-circles` config: `{ data, name, value, unit?, format?, title?, subtitle? }`. Or a full spec.

sideAt.description: Position on the scale where the `side` graphic starts. Default: under the last figure.

height.description: Height of the scale in px. Default: 68px per item, at least 920 (760 when stacked).

scorecard.title: Scorecard
scorecard.description: A recurring report. It has a masthead with the report name and period, a headline that states the main change, a KPI grid with changes and sparklines, a ranked list beside one or two trend charts, an optional comparison table, short notes and a source note. Use: Use it for weekly or monthly numbers. Keep the layout the same in every edition so readers know where each number is. Change the headline each edition to state the main change with its number. The headline and the KPI row should be enough for a reader who stops there. The ranking, trends and notes add detail. Highlight the one row or series the headline is about and leave the rest grey. Avoid: A one-off finding (use `executive-brief`). Readers who need to filter the data themselves (use `data-explorer`). More than six KPIs.

social-card.title: Social card
social-card.description: A graphic that states one fact, at a fixed aspect ratio (1:1, 4:5, 16:9 or 9:16). It has a kicker, a headline, one exhibit, a source and a credit, painted on the theme surface. A button downloads the whole card as a PNG. Use: Use it for one finding that will be shared in a feed, a slide or a chat thread with no text around it. State the fact with its number in the headline. Use one simple exhibit, such as one highlighted bar, one line or one number. Put the source and your name on the card, because it will be shared without the page. Use 1:1 or 4:5 for feeds, 16:9 for slides and link previews, 9:16 for stories. Avoid: More than one fact or more than one exhibit (use `story-deck` for a sequence, `executive-brief` for a page). Charts that need a legend, small labels or hovering to read, because a shared image is not interactive. An exhibit with its own `title`, because the card's headline is the title.

story-deck.title: Story deck
story-deck.description: A sequence of full-frame cards (title, stat, chart, quote, closing) that the reader swipes or steps through. Each card states one fact. It has an optional fixed aspect ratio, a keyboard-accessible pager and a stacked layout for print. Use: Use it for a short sequence read on a phone, such as a “year in review”. Each card should be readable in a couple of seconds. State the main fact with its number on the title card. Put one fact on each later card, as a number or as one chart with one highlighted mark under a headline that states the fact. Use five to ten cards. End with a closing card and the sources. Charts in cards should have few data points and direct labels, with no legend. Avoid: Findings that need two exhibits in view at once (use `executive-brief`). A single shareable image (use `social-card`). Dense charts or long paragraphs, because a card has little room. One chart that changes step by step (use `scrolly-chart` in `steps` mode).

cards.description: The cards in order. Each has a `kind`: `title` `{ title, deck?, byline? }`; `stat` `{ value, label, context?, delta?, deltaLabel?, upIsGood?, format?, text? }`; `chart` `{ title, chart, text? }`; `quote` `{ quote, attribution?, role? }`; `closing` `{ title, text?, points?, action?: { label, href } }`. Any card takes `kicker`, `tone: "surface" | "inverse" | "accent"` and `id`.

aspect.description: Shape of every card. `auto` lets cards take the height their content needs. `16:9` falls back to `4:5` in containers under 520px.

timeline-poster.title: Timeline poster
timeline-poster.description: A poster of change over a run of periods: a full-width ribbon of bands whose thickness is each entity's value and whose order is its rank (`ribbon-chart`), a strip of two to four dated figures under it, and a bottom row with one measure per period as thick bars (`block-bar`) and one share at several dates as nested outlines (`nested-shares`). Use: Use it when the subject is how 4 to 8 named things grew, shrank and changed places over 4 to 10 periods: electricity by source, library loans by format, commuters by mode. Give `hero` the periods and entities, `milestones` the dated numbers a reader should take away, `bars` one measure of the whole at each period and `shares` one share at a few dates. State the latest value in the title. Avoid: A single series over time (use `line-chart` or `area-chart` in a `poster`). Events with start and end dates (use `timeline-chart` or the `timeline-story` template). More than 8 entities or 10 periods, because the bands get too thin to label. Positions on one scale (use `scale-poster`). Parts of one subject at one date (use `radial-poster`).

hero.description: The hero: one band per entity across the periods, drawn by `ribbon-chart`. Wide rows take `y` as a list of columns; long rows take `y` and `series`. A full spec or element replaces it.

milestones.description: Two to four dated figures in a strip under the hero, in time order. `at` is the period, printed in small capitals over the figure.

bars.description: Bottom left: one measure at each period as thick bars with the numbers inside (`block-bar`). `marker: { after, label }` draws a dotted line after one period to mark an event.

shares.description: Bottom right: one share at 2 to 8 dates as outlines nested in one square (`nested-shares`). `format` defaults to `"{value}%"`. With only one of `bars` and `shares`, that one takes the full width.

timeline-story.title: Timeline story
timeline-story.description: A story told in date order. It has a headline, one overview exhibit of the whole period (a timeline chart or an annotated line), dated chapters along a rail, a closing paragraph and a source note. Each chapter has a short text and an optional small exhibit. Use: Use it when the reader needs the events in date order to understand a change. State the change over the whole period in the headline, with the numbers and dates. Mark the main events on the overview exhibit as annotations. Give each chapter one event. Add a small figure to a chapter only when it has a number to show. Mark the two or three most important events with `emphasis`. Avoid: Events with no measure that runs through the period (use a plain `annotated-timeline`). A comparison of two states with nothing in between (use `comparison-brief`). More than eight chapters. Merge minor events into the text of the chapter before or after.

visual-essay.title: Visual essay
visual-essay.description: A long article read by scrolling. It has a headline, then an ordered list of blocks in a reading column, then a source note. The blocks are prose, figures, charts with a callout, scrolly sequences, pull quotes, stat rows, small multiples and chapter breaks. Exhibits can be wider than the column. Use: Use it for a finding that takes several charts and some text to explain. State the main finding with its number in the headline. Put the main figure within the first screen. Alternate text and charts, with two or three short paragraphs before each exhibit. In a scrolly block change one thing per step, such as the highlight, the year or an annotation. Use one accent colour for the subject in every chart. Avoid: A summary for someone who will not scroll (use `executive-brief`). Reference material read out of order (use `report-page`). More than one or two scrolly blocks. Use one only where the chart changes between steps.

kicker.description: Small label above the title.

date.description: Publication date. ISO dates are formatted for the locale.

blocks.description: The story in reading order. Each block has a `kind`: `prose` `{ text, lead? }`; `figure` `{ chart, caption? }`; `callout` `{ chart, lead, body, label?, tone?, side? }`; `scrolly` `{ chart, steps, cumulative?, scrollMode?, side?, stepHeight? }` (the props of `scrolly-chart`); `quote` `{ quote, attribution?, role? }`; `stats` `{ items, title? }`; `multiples` `{ facet, ... }` (props of `small-multiples`, or of `small-multiple-grid` when it has a `chart`); `break` `{ title, step?, total?, text? }`. Any block takes `width: "text" | "wide" | "full"` and an `id`. A bare chart spec is treated as a wide figure.
